title: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs
authors: Tasnin Tabassum Ali, Faisal Ahmed, Muhammad Anwarul Azim
abstract: Timely access to appropriate medical specialists remains a bottleneck in Bangladesh's healthcare system, as patients describe symptoms in informal Bangla rather than clinical terms, leading to ineffective referrals. This paper compares four model families for predicting medical specialties from Bangla patient narratives: six machine learning (ML) models using hybrid TF-IDF features, four deep learning (DL) models using Word2Vec embeddings trained on the corpus, four fine-tuned transformers, and five large language models (LLMs) evaluated zero-shot. From a corpus of 3798 patient records covering 20 specialties, we retained the five with the most records (Medicine, Gynecology, Dermatology, Pediatrics, Gastroenterology) and split the resulting 2730 records 80:20 into training and test sets shared by all families. The best transformer was XLM-RoBERTa (86.26% accuracy, 86.21% macro-F1), the best ML model was SVM (84.98%, 84.92%), the best DL model was Bidirectional GRU (80.77%, 80.83%), and the best LLM was Gemini (90.29%, 90.15%). Holm-corrected paired McNemar tests show SVM significantly outperforming Bi-LSTM (adjusted p = 0.004), whereas the Gemini-versus-Grok gap does not survive correction (adjusted p = 0.104), and neither the strongest transformer versus the weakest LLM (Grok) nor SVM versus the strongest transformer reaches significance. A tuned classical model is thus statistically indistinguishable from the strongest transformer, so accuracy rankings alone should not be read as evidence of one family's superiority. The findings provide a comparative baseline for Bangla medical text classification.

infographic.key_insight: Gemini had the highest observed accuracy (90.29%), but SVM and the best transformer were not statistically distinguishable in this Bangla specialty-classification study.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Classifying informal Bangla patient narratives could support referral workflows, but this study does not establish clinical safety or improved patient outcomes.
method: Retained 2,730 patient records across the five most represented medical specialties.
Compared six ML models, four deep learning models, four fine-tuned transformers, and five zero-shot LLMs using a shared 80:20 train–test split.
Evaluated accuracy and macro-F1, with Holm-corrected paired McNemar tests for model comparisons.
infographic.evidence_signal: Leading accuracy/macro-F1 scores were Gemini 90.29%/90.15%, XLM-RoBERTa 86.26%/86.21%, SVM 84.98%/84.92%, and Bidirectional GRU 80.77%/80.83%.
infographic.watch_item: Restricting evaluation to five of the original 20 specialties limits generalizability to broader referral settings.
infographic.paper_title: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs

title: InterGenEHR$^+$: An Interactive Framework for Natural Language-Conditioned Generation of Longitudinal Patient Trajectories
authors: Yu Yang, Jiafeng Song, Baraa F Abed, Christina Creel, Sagar B Dave, Henry Foote
abstract: Objective: To develop and validate InterGenEHR$^+$, an interactive framework for natural language-conditioned generation of synthetic tabular electronic health records (EHRs) and longitudinal trajectories for scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models. Methods: An optional large language model (LLM) parser converts clinical requests into structured constraints. Conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records, while diffusion models generate longitudinal trajectories. We evaluate parsing, distributional fidelity, imputation, clinical-constraint adherence, mortality prediction, and clinical plausibility using a multi-institutional cohort of 874 patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO). Results: Gemma 3 4B with few-shot prompting achieves the highest parsing performance with a low spurious slot rate. IGE-TabDDPM and IGE-PMVAE perform well in single-time-point generation; IGE-CSDI, IGE-FGTI, and IGE-MTSCI lead on different longitudinal fidelity metrics. Across five random seeds and three classifiers, synthetic cohorts retain predictive utility for mortality prediction on real test data. Clinician ratings support trajectory plausibility and alignment with requested scenarios. Conclusion: InterGenEHR$^+$ supports clinician-specified generation of EHR trajectories with statistical fidelity and downstream predictive utility in the evaluated VV-ECMO cohort. Extension to other clinical settings requires further validation. Significance: The framework supports scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models in data-sparse critical care settings.

infographic.key_insight: InterGenEHR+ generates synthetic EHR records and longitudinal patient trajectories conditioned on natural-language clinical scenarios.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models in data-sparse critical care settings.
method: An optional LLM parser translates clinical requests into structured constraints.
Conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records.
Diffusion models generate longitudinal trajectories.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation in a multi-institutional cohort of 874 VV-ECMO patients assessed fidelity, constraint adherence, and clinician-rated plausibility; across five seeds and three classifiers, synthetic cohorts retained mortality-prediction utility on real test data.
infographic.watch_item: Findings are limited to the evaluated VV-ECMO cohort; other clinical settings require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: InterGenEHR$^+$: An Interactive Framework for Natural Language-Conditioned Generation of Longitudinal Patient Trajectories

title: JHealthBench-L: Clinician-Reviewed Localization of HealthBench for Rubric-Based Medical LLM Evaluation in Japan
authors: Shohei Hisada, Keisuke Orimo, Kenji Igarashi, Kota Sato, Masahiro Kazama, Mitsuhisa Ota
abstract: Rubric-based benchmarks such as HealthBench evaluate large language models (LLMs) on open-ended health consultations using case-specific physician criteria, many of which presuppose the healthcare institutions, medications, and care pathways of their source region. Under machine translation alone, these regional assumptions remain in the rubric, leaving responses appropriate in Japan uncredited or falsely penalized under foreign clinical rules. To adapt established clinical evaluation perspectives to Japan without authoring rubrics from scratch, we construct JHealthBench-L (79 patient-facing consultations, 1,022 criteria) through source-cited LLM drafting, single-specialist selection and revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review. Specialists rewrote only 4.4% of criteria from scratch, and independent reviewers approved 93.6% of Stage-2 criteria without issue. Comparing JHealthBench-L with a machine-translated baseline across 18 LLMs reveals that translation-only evaluation preserves coarse model rankings ($τ= 0.817$, mean shift +0.027) yet flips verdicts on 17.7% of modified criteria (vs. 7.3% re-grading noise) and reduces false penalties on Japan-adapted negative criteria by 7.1 percentage points, masking item-level clinical mismeasurement behind stable leaderboards. Axis-level and paired analyses further show that context awareness and Japan-specific clinical criteria remain primary bottlenecks, whereas Japanese continual pretraining and reasoning post-training substantially improve locally grounded performance. Datasets, physician revision logs, and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/horshohei/JHealthBench-L.

infographic.key_insight: Localizing medical evaluation rubrics for Japan revealed errors hidden by broadly stable LLM rankings under translation-only evaluation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Japan-specific rubrics can better recognize responses aligned with local healthcare institutions, medications, and care pathways.
method: Adapted 79 patient-facing consultations with 1,022 evaluation criteria.
Combined source-cited LLM drafting, specialist revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review.
Compared localized and machine-translated rubrics across 18 LLMs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Rankings remained broadly stable (τ=0.817), but verdicts flipped on 17.7% of modified criteria versus 7.3% re-grading noise; localization reduced false penalties on Japan-adapted negative criteria by 7.1 percentage points.
infographic.watch_item: Results from 79 benchmark consultations do not establish safety or effectiveness in real-world patient care.
infographic.paper_title: JHealthBench-L: Clinician-Reviewed Localization of HealthBench for Rubric-Based Medical LLM Evaluation in Japan

title: TAT-Det: A Dataset for Testicular Appendage Torsion Detection and Segmentation in Ultrasound Images
authors: Ying Jiang, Juntao Jiang, Linxuan Fan, Lingling Li, Yaqi Wang, Xiuzhen Yang
abstract: Background: Testicular appendage torsion (TAT) is the leading cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal children. Yet, its diagnosis remains challenging due to nonspecific clinical manifestations and the absence of standardized datasets for pediatric acute scrotal emergencies. Results: We present TAT-Det, an expert-annotated ultrasound dataset specifically designed for TAT. TAT-Det comprises 2,600 ultrasound images from 1,203 patients collected at the Children's Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine. Each TAT-positive image is accompanied by lesion-level bounding boxes for detection and pixel-level segmentation masks for fine-grained delineation. Annotations were produced through a multi-stage workflow involving independent annotation by board-certified pediatric sonographers, consensus review, and refinement. Baseline benchmarks for object detection and semantic segmentation using representative deep learning models are further provided, with YOLO11m achieving the best detection performance and RWKV-UNet the best segmentation performance. Conclusions: TAT-Det addresses the lack of publicly available resources for pediatric emergency ultrasound and establishes a foundation for developing and evaluating artificial intelligence methods for automated TAT analysis.

infographic.key_insight: TAT-Det provides expert-annotated ultrasound images to support AI detection and segmentation of testicular appendage torsion.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The dataset supports research on a leading cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal children, where diagnosis can be challenging.
method: Collected 2,600 ultrasound images from 1,203 patients at one children's hospital.
Annotated TAT-positive images with lesion bounding boxes and pixel-level segmentation masks.
Used independent expert annotation, consensus review, and refinement; benchmarked detection and segmentation models.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among the benchmarked models, YOLO11m performed best for detection and RWKV-UNet for segmentation; the abstract reports no numerical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Single-center data may limit generalizability; performance across other hospitals and ultrasound systems needs evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: TAT-Det: A Dataset for Testicular Appendage Torsion Detection and Segmentation in Ultrasound Images

title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization
authors: Ilkin Masimov, Rufana Baghirli, Muhammad Rashid
abstract: Background: Large language models produce hallucinations in medical question answering (QA). Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard mitigation, but evaluations almost universally treat the verifier's output as ground truth, an assumption rarely tested. Objective: To measure, claim by claim against human judgement, how such a pipeline fails in a guideline-grounded clinical setting. Methods: We built a dataset of 160 questions (100 patient vignettes from 89 de-identified cases, 60 fact-based) over four recent ESC cardiology guidelines, all approved by a practising internist, and a retrieval corpus of 627 hand-verified guideline records at two chunk granularities. A five-stage pipeline was run under four retrieval configurations and three independent runs (1920 arm-runs); all 606 first-pass refuted claims were manually audited, an independent judge re-judged 906 decisions, and the expert blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims. Results: Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations. Correction loops converged in 85.2-95.1% of cases, yet 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by correction. Single-run true-hallucination recall was 35.6-41.2%, the three-run union 71-80%; verifier agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.505). The blind probe estimated the accepted-claim miss rate at 3.2% (95% CI 0.7-6.7%). Final genuine-error rate: 1.7% of answers. Conclusion: Claim-level verification reduces hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability, not generation, is the limiting factor and must be measured, not assumed.

infographic.key_insight: Guideline-grounded claim verification reduced hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability remained the main bottleneck.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For cardiology QA tools, automated verification can reduce errors but should not be treated as proof that an answer is clinically correct.
method: Built 160 internist-approved questions across four ESC cardiology guidelines and 627 hand-verified retrieval records.
Tested a five-stage verify-and-revise pipeline across four retrieval configurations and three independent runs.
Manually audited 606 flagged claims, independently re-judged 906 decisions, and blindly expert-reviewed 100 accepted claims.
infographic.evidence_signal: Only 44.7–50.6% of flagged claims were genuine hallucinations; final genuine errors affected 1.7% of answers, with 35% of genuine final errors introduced by correction.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to this guideline-grounded benchmark; single-run hallucination recall was only 35.6–41.2%, so automated acceptance can still miss errors.
infographic.paper_title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization

title: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages
authors: Samah Fodeh, Sreeraj Ramachandran, Ganesh Puthiaraju, Sarah Schellhorn
abstract: Objectives: Patient portal messages provide invaluable information about communication dynamics between patients and healthcare providers, but extracting it manually is labor-intensive. We developed and evaluated EPPC-CARE, an automated framework for identifying communication behaviors together with the supporting text for each classification. Materials and Methods: From 867 messages, we obtained 5,516 reference standard annotations. Each annotation is a triplet of communication-related text (span), a broader communication category (Code), and a specific subcategory (Sub-code). We evaluated EPPC-CARE's identified triplets across six open-weight large language models (LLMs) against supervised fine-tuning and communication-based models such as EPPC-OASIS. We also compared EPPC-CARE with human expert annotations on 100 messages. Results: EPPC-CARE improved performance over EPPC-OASIS across all six models. EPPC-CARE's Triplet F1 improved by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%. On the human expert evaluation subset, EPPC-CARE and the human expert showed comparable agreement with the reference standard, with differences favoring EPPC-CARE. Discussion: These findings suggest that identifying triplet components (span, code, subcode) sequentially can improve performance across model families while preserving the supporting text behind each identification. EPPC-CARE links the communication code and subcode with the source text (span), supporting human verification of automated annotations in clinical informatics. EPPC-CARE may therefore make larger-scale studies of patient-provider communication more feasible and provide a foundation for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows. Conclusion: EPPC-CARE offers a more reliable and reviewable approach for automated characterization of communication behaviors in secure patient-provider messaging.

infographic.key_insight: EPPC-CARE identifies communication behaviors in patient-provider messages while linking each label to supporting text for human review.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support larger-scale research on patient-provider communication and human-in-the-loop annotation workflows.
method: Sequentially identifies supporting text spans, broad communication categories, and specific subcategories.
Evaluated across six open-weight LLMs against supervised fine-tuning and communication-focused approaches.
Compared with human expert annotations on a 100-message subset.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 5,516 reference annotations from 867 messages, EPPC-CARE improved Triplet F1 over EPPC-OASIS by 2.90 percentage points on average, reaching a best score of 64.4%.
infographic.watch_item: The reported performance leaves substantial annotation error, and generalizability beyond the evaluated messages remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages

title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study
authors: Neda Ghafouri
abstract: As clinical AI agents begin to interact with electronic health records (EHRs), large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate their actions. But how reliably can these judges recognize clinically dangerous mistakes, especially when an agent appears to have completed its task successfully? We investigate this question using MedAgentBench by introducing controlled clinical errors into verified agent trajectories. The experiments include 416 faulty trajectories, eight error categories, and six open-weight LLM judges. By comparing each faulty trajectory with its correct counterpart, we measure whether judges genuinely recognize errors rather than simply flagging more actions as unsafe. The findings show that access to clinical evidence significantly improves judge reliability. When shown only the final answer, judges cannot distinguish errors that leave it unchanged, while flagging 56% of correct trajectories. With full trajectory information, the ability to distinguish unsafe actions from correct ones reaches a score of 0.75, and providing actual EHR responses improves discrimination by 0.39. Surprisingly, including the agent's reasoning does not improve overall performance and reduces detection of incorrectly reported clinical values by 0.18, which remain the hardest errors to detect. MedGemma performed worse than the general-purpose model and was the only judge to miss potentially dangerous medication overdoses. We also find that the benchmark's original grader accepts all 38 trajectories with an intentionally skipped laboratory check, while combining LLM judges with a rule-based checker informed by the full EHR record detects 97% of injected faults.

infographic.key_insight: LLM judges detect unsafe clinical actions more reliably when given EHR evidence; apparent task completion alone is not a dependable safety signal.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Evaluating EHR-connected AI agents should assess their underlying actions and clinical evidence, not just their final answers.
method: Injected eight categories of clinical errors into verified MedAgentBench trajectories.
Compared 416 faulty trajectories with correct counterparts using six open-weight LLM judges.
Tested different evidence inputs and combined LLM judgments with an EHR-informed rule-based checker.
infographic.evidence_signal: Final-answer-only judges flagged 56% of correct trajectories, while full-trajectory evaluation reached a discrimination score of 0.75 and combined LLM–rule-based checking detected 97% of injected faults.
infographic.watch_item: These controlled benchmark results do not establish real-world clinical safety; added agent reasoning did not improve overall detection, and incorrectly reported clinical values remained hardest to detect.
infographic.paper_title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study

title: Laya-IsoToken: Day-One Clinical Codebook Switching via Closed-Form Operator Compilation
authors: Zeqiang Wang
abstract: Healthcare systems periodically revise diagnostic and procedural classifications (ICD-9 to ICD-10/11), update hospital reimbursement groupers (MS-DRG), and deploy clinical coding across languages. Supervised coding networks bind clinical text encoders to fixed per-code classifier weights, forcing hospitals to re-annotate tens of thousands of records before switching codebooks, whereas standalone large language models incur high latency and hallucinate invalid codes. Here we show that day-one clinical codebook switching becomes feasible without target-labeled notes when local clinical evidence reading is decoupled from a strictly frozen multilingual concept space. Laya-IsoToken trains a clinical span reader once on source records with zero per-code classifier parameters, separating text evidence from historical disease prevalence. Given only public target code descriptions, closed-form matrix compilation aligns distributional shifts, compensates for paraphrased definitions, and deduplicates sibling codes in under three seconds, while a pre-deployment geometric residual routes unfamiliar concepts to offline language model verification. Across 32,804 MIMIC-IV ICD-9 discharges, Laya-IsoToken matches published supervised baselines (62.6% Micro-F1) while reducing active calibration error by 32%. Switched with zero target training notes to 13,783 unseen-patient ICD-10 discharges, MS-DRG groups, and multilingual cohorts, it outperforms biomedical dense retrievers, semantic crosswalks (+5.4 F1 points on ICD-10, paired $d_z = 0.49$, $p < 0.001$), and official US CMS equivalence mappings (+3.5 points, $p < 0.001$) at 9.4 ms per admission. Pairing this reader with an offline 31B verifier across 1,000 full discharge summaries lifts zero-training ICD-10 coding to 40.6% Micro-F1 (57.0% category F1, $d_z = 0.66$, $p < 0.001$) with 0.0% invalid code hallucinations.

infographic.key_insight: Laya-IsoToken enables clinical coding systems to switch codebooks without target-labeled training notes by separating text evidence extraction from code definitions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could reduce annotation burden when hospitals update diagnostic classifications, reimbursement groupers, or coding languages.
method: Train a clinical span reader once, using a frozen multilingual concept space and no per-code classifier parameters.
Compile public target code descriptions into alignment operators in under three seconds.
Route unfamiliar concepts to offline language-model verification using a geometric residual.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 62.6% Micro-F1 on 32,804 ICD-9 discharges, a 5.4-point ICD-10 F1 gain over semantic crosswalks on unseen patients, and 40.6% ICD-10 Micro-F1 with offline verification on 1,000 summaries.
infographic.watch_item: Real-world generalizability and workflow impact require prospective evaluation; zero invalid codes in the reported verifier evaluation does not establish coding accuracy or clinical safety.
infographic.paper_title: Laya-IsoToken: Day-One Clinical Codebook Switching via Closed-Form Operator Compilation

title: The ITE-Transformer: A pre-trained foundation model for predicting individualized treatment effects from electronic health records
authors: Arceri, C.; Angelis, E.; Heesen, P.; Melnychuk, V.; Bendszus, M.; Bauer, S.; Feuerriegel, S.
abstract: Transformer-based foundation models have shown strong potential for modeling longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), yet existing models focus primarily on risk prediction rather than treatment effect estimation, which limits evidence generation. Here, we introduce the ITE-Transformer, a transformer-based framework that combines self-supervised representation learning from longitudinal patient trajectories with doubly robust causal machine learning for predicting individualized treatment effects (ITEs). As a result, our ITE-Transformer allows to study counterfactual questions of how an individual patients outcome may differ under alternative treatment strategies. The ITE-Transformer learns temporally contextualized representations of patients diagnosis and medication histories and subsequently uses these representations to predict treatment assignment, treatment-specific outcome risks, and patient-specific ITEs. The ITE-Transformer is trained using structured EHR data from[~] 350,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program and evaluated in two clinically different comparative-effectiveness tasks: (i) GLP-1 receptor agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors among patients with type 2 diabetes, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome, and (ii) immunotherapy versus chemotherapy in a pan-cancer cohort, with all-cause mortality as the outcome. Across both applications, the ITE-Transformer improves the discrimination and calibration of treatment assignment and outcome models compared with existing tabular machine learning approaches and an otherwise identical transformer trained without self-supervised pre-training. The ITE-Transformer further identifies substantial heterogeneity in predicted ITEs and yields interpretable patterns of treatment response associated with patients diagnoses, medication histories, and comorbidities. Together, our work demonstrates how clinical foundation models can be developed for analyzing heterogeneity in treatment effects and thus support real-world evidence generation.

infographic.key_insight: The ITE-Transformer combines EHR pre-training with causal machine learning to estimate how treatment effects may differ across individual patients.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support real-world comparative-effectiveness research by identifying patient characteristics associated with predicted treatment benefit.
method: Self-supervised transformer pre-training on longitudinal diagnosis and medication histories.
Prediction of treatment assignment and treatment-specific outcome risks from patient representations.
Doubly robust causal machine learning to estimate individualized treatment effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using structured EHRs from approximately 350,000 All of Us participants, evaluation in diabetes and pan-cancer cohorts showed better treatment-assignment and outcome-model discrimination and calibration than tabular models and a transformer without pre-training.
infographic.watch_item: Improved predictive performance does not establish accurate individual causal effects; observational estimates remain dependent on confounding and other causal assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: The ITE-Transformer: A pre-trained foundation model for predicting individualized treatment effects from electronic health records

title: ASCENT: A Benchmark for Evaluating and Advancing Stepwise Diagnostic Reasoning in Large Language Models on Common Clinical Scenarios
authors: Yera Choi, Yeong Hwa Kim, Jaedeok Lee, Taekang Kim, Sangdoo Yun, Seong-Eun Moon
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at medical question answering yet are rarely evaluated on the stepwise diagnostic reasoning that defines real clinical workflows, where impressions are revised as information accumulates. We build Annotated Stepwise Clinical rEasoning for NaturalisTic Diagnosis (ASCENT), a clinician-annotated benchmark and training resource of 3,078 stepwise problems derived from MedQA-USMLE that decomposes each vignette into EMR-aligned steps (Findings, Impression, supporting Rationale), enabling evaluation of intermediate reasoning under incomplete information. Experiments and training with ASCENT revealed insights into how current LLMs handle stepwise diagnostic reasoning. Even strong reasoning models that perform well on MedQA-USMLE leave substantial headroom on ASCENT, and general-purpose frontier models trail further, exposing a persistent gap between fully informed and stepwise diagnosis. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and 32B on ASCENT yields measurable F1 gains over both pre-trained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT-trained baselines, with gains driven primarily by precision. Complementary robustness analyses (counterfactual perturbation, format-vs-content control, judge agreement, and rollout) further show that ASCENT-fine-tuned models rely on the diagnostic content of prior impressions rather than imitating their output format, while error propagation under rollout remains a key challenge for clinical deployment.

infographic.key_insight: ASCENT exposes gaps in LLMs’ stepwise diagnostic reasoning that standard medical question answering can miss, while targeted fine-tuning improves performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Evaluating how models revise diagnostic impressions as information accumulates better reflects clinical workflows, but does not establish readiness for patient care.
method: Built 3,078 clinician-annotated stepwise problems from MedQA-USMLE.
Organized vignettes into EMR-aligned findings, impressions, and supporting rationales.
Evaluated models, fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B and 32B, and tested robustness.
infographic.evidence_signal: ASCENT fine-tuning improved F1 over pre-trained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT-trained baselines, primarily through precision gains; even strong reasoning models showed substantial room for improvement.
infographic.watch_item: Errors can propagate across sequential diagnostic steps, and benchmark gains do not demonstrate real-world clinical safety or effectiveness.
infographic.paper_title: ASCENT: A Benchmark for Evaluating and Advancing Stepwise Diagnostic Reasoning in Large Language Models on Common Clinical Scenarios

title: A dataset of clinically similar image pairs from citation-linked case reports for medical image retrieval
authors: Guy Shmueli, Keno K. Bressem, Tom Hope
abstract: Retrieving images of patients clinically similar to a given patient can support diagnosis, teaching and research. Training and evaluating retrieval systems requires knowing which images of different patients show the same finding, and existing datasets are small or narrow in scope. We construct PMC-PaIR, a dataset of 86,144 pairs of clinically similar images from 56,013 open-access PubMed Central case reports, which often document rare or challenging presentations. We develop an approach that follows citations, which often link case reports of similar patients. To determine what two linked cases share clinically, it prompts large language models to generate and answer hierarchical questions, from modality to diagnosis and findings, and to match images by caption using the answers. Experts find the pairs highly accurate, and this question-guided approach finds twice as many correct pairs as direct matching. Fine-tuning BiomedCLIP on PMC-PaIR improves retrieval in all modality, anatomy and diagnosis categories tested, for image-only queries and image queries with a short text naming the finding. We release the dataset and the automated pipeline, which can extend PMC-PaIR as new case reports are published.

infographic.key_insight: PMC-PaIR uses citation-linked case reports and question-guided language models to build clinically similar image pairs that improve medical image retrieval.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Retrieving images with similar clinical findings could support diagnosis, teaching and research, but clinical benefit was not evaluated.
method: Follow citations between open-access PubMed Central case reports to identify potentially similar cases.
Use language models to ask and answer hierarchical questions about modality, diagnosis and findings, then match images using captions.
Fine-tune BiomedCLIP on the resulting image pairs and evaluate retrieval.
infographic.evidence_signal: The dataset contains 86,144 image pairs from 56,013 case reports; experts judged pairs highly accurate, question-guided matching found twice as many correct pairs as direct matching, and fine-tuning improved retrieval across all tested categories.
infographic.watch_item: Case reports often feature rare or challenging presentations, so generalization to routine clinical imaging needs further evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: A dataset of clinically similar image pairs from citation-linked case reports for medical image retrieval

title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence
authors: Sage-Med Team, :, Ming Hu, Cheng Tang, Wei Li, Rongbin Li
abstract: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.

infographic.key_insight: Sage-Med-Preview reports stronger medical multimodal performance through progressive training, while model-size scaling alone mainly improves text capabilities.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings may inform medical AI research on image understanding, report generation, and visual grounding, but do not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: 35B-parameter multimodal model with 3B activated parameters.
Stage-specific data curation over 322.7 million candidate records.
Medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation against 77 competing models covered 238 tasks across 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks; the reported average on 31 public multimodal benchmarks was 58.26%, versus 50.99% for Hulu-Med-235B-A22B and 52.24% for Intern-S2-Preview.
infographic.watch_item: Complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows remain challenging; benchmark gains do not establish clinical safety or patient benefit.
infographic.paper_title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence

title: BayesPath: Reliability-Aware Bayesian Reasoning for Whole-Slide Pathology Agents
authors: Bryan Wong, Xun Xu, Jongwoo Kim, Huazhu Fu, Nancy F. Chen, Mun Yong Yi
abstract: Diagnosing whole-slide images (WSIs) requires hypothesis-driven reasoning: pathologists form a differential diagnosis, seek discriminative evidence, weigh its reliability, and stop once it suffices. However, existing training-free WSI agents lack an explicit framework for such reasoning. They typically use a large language model (LLM) to aggregate the region descriptions of a multimodal LLM (MLLM), without a belief over the candidates or regard for the descriptions' reliability. Consequently, a repeated model error counts as independent evidence for an incorrect diagnosis. We introduce BayesPath, a training-free WSI agent that casts the pathologist's Scan-Look-Weigh-Decide process as reliability-aware Bayesian reasoning. An explicit belief over the candidates is updated with each observation through a reliability-aware likelihood and guides where to look next and when to stop. This likelihood corrects for the models' answer bias, discounts correlated observations, and captures diagnostic confusions estimated without labels. The updates form an interpretable evidence trail of how each observation shapes the belief. On five MultiPathQA tasks spanning slide classification and slide VQA, BayesPath achieves the highest average accuracy among training-free agents, 58.6% against 34.1% for the next best, with large gains on slide classification. On identical observations, Bayesian updating outperforms LLM aggregation on average, even with a larger LLM. BayesPath's belief is also better calibrated than naive Bayes, so uncertain cases can be deferred to pathologists. Code is available at https://github.com/bryanwong17/BayesPath

infographic.key_insight: BayesPath improves training-free whole-slide pathology reasoning by tracking diagnostic beliefs and discounting unreliable or correlated AI observations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Its interpretable evidence trail and calibrated uncertainty could support pathology review and flag uncertain cases for pathologist assessment.
method: Uses a Scan–Look–Weigh–Decide loop to guide region selection and stopping.
Updates candidate beliefs through reliability-aware Bayesian inference.
Corrects answer bias, discounts correlated observations, and models diagnostic confusions estimated without labels.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five MultiPathQA slide-classification and slide-VQA tasks, BayesPath achieved 58.6% average accuracy versus 34.1% for the next-best training-free agent.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark gains do not establish clinical safety or generalizability; real-world validation is needed before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: BayesPath: Reliability-Aware Bayesian Reasoning for Whole-Slide Pathology Agents

title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle
authors: Pui Chung Siu, Yuan Liang, Claudia Cabrera, Mani Mudaliar, Arkaitz Zubiaga
abstract: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. We recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event, the pair's first clinical trial. This lets us test whether a language model can forecast such events after its training cutoff, rather than recall events before it. We rebuild a dated biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 up to its newest version. We then ask six open language models, with and without this graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease the next year. Without retrieval, the models rank about as well as trial history, a count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, also after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain, before or after the models' training cutoffs. The newest graph raises five of six models clearly above that baseline, but its paths usually include the answer: the pair's own trial, dated after the decision. Evaluations of target prioritisation should date both features and labels, with evidence from before the decision and outcomes after it.

infographic.key_insight: Apparent gains in drug-target forecasting may reflect access to future trial records rather than genuine predictive ability.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Reliable target prioritisation could inform which hypotheses enter costly clinical trials, but this study cautions against interpreting leaked outcomes as forecasting success.
method: Defined each target–disease event as the pair’s first clinical trial.
Reconstructed year-end biomedical knowledge graphs from 2020 onward.
Tested six open language models with and without graph retrieval against a trial-history baseline.
infographic.evidence_signal: Pre-decision evidence added at most small gains, while the newest graph clearly lifted five of six models above baseline but usually included the target–disease pair’s own future trial.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluations must restrict evidence to information available before the decision and assess outcomes occurring afterward to prevent temporal leakage.
infographic.paper_title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle

title: EATS: Scaling Tool-Use Experience for Medical Reasoning Agents
authors: Mingyuan Li, Tong Jia, Haoran Wang, Wenbo Qi, Ziyuan Yang, Bowen Ma
abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.

infographic.key_insight: EATS improves medical agents’ tool selection by retrieving relevant past tool-use experiences rather than relying only on tool descriptions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: More effective use of specialized tools could support medical image question answering and report generation, but clinical benefit remains unproven.
method: Store queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback in an experience memory.
Retrieve relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries.
Expand memory through test-time interactions without ground-truth supervision.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four public datasets—ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA—and three multimodal LLMs, the abstract reports consistent gains in tool selection and downstream task performance, without numerical effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Self-evaluated feedback may preserve errors in memory; reliability under clinical distribution shifts needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: EATS: Scaling Tool-Use Experience for Medical Reasoning Agents

title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data
authors: Merel Kuijs, Till Richter, Rushin H. Gindra, Korbinian Traeuble, Christian Matek, Rebeka Luknárová
abstract: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder with a cross-modal latent alignment mechanism, CAMEO learns shared representations requiring only minimal paired samples. Evaluated on computational pathology tasks such as niche classification and cell type composition prediction, CAMEO achieves superior data efficiency, outperforming contrastive approaches like CLIP in low paired-data regimes, and highlighting the benefits of adversarial alignment when paired annotations are scarce. To facilitate further research, we additionally release a fully annotated HuggingFace dataset comprising three organs and paired image and gene expression modalities. By extending fusion methods to address limited pairing and small-scale datasets, we provide a framework that advances multimodal learning and broadens its applicability to real-world biomedical problems.

infographic.key_insight: CAMEO learns shared multimodal representations from small, partially paired datasets, outperforming CLIP-like contrastive approaches when paired samples are scarce.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support biomedical research combining pathology images and gene expression when matched samples are limited, but clinical utility is not established.
method: Uses pre-trained unimodal encoders.
Applies adversarial cross-modal latent alignment.
Learns shared representations with minimal paired samples.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluations on niche classification and cell type composition prediction, plus a released annotated dataset spanning three organs with paired images and gene expression.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative performance estimates or evidence of clinical validation.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data

title: Confidence-Based Adaptive Retrieval Fails Where It Matters Most: A Paradox in Biomedical Question Answering
authors: Chengying She, Siyu Deng, Haiyan Ge, Lizhuang Liu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for biomedical question answering, but plausible incorrect answers remain a safety risk in clinical settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can ground responses in medical literature, while confidence-based adaptive RAG retrieves only when the model appears uncertain. We evaluate this routing strategy on three biomedical QA benchmarks of increasing difficulty and compare models across a broad range of parameter scales. The results reveal a paradox: confidence is well calibrated (AUROC 0.78--0.89) on standard medical exam questions where retrieval adds little value (+2.4\% to -1.4\%), yet becomes \emph{near-random} (AUROC 0.506) on specialist-level questions where retrieval helps most (+11.2\%). Five uncertainty signals---first-token probability, margin, entropy, consistency-based sampling, and verbalized confidence---show the same failure pattern. Five post-hoc calibration correction strategies, including density-ratio reweighting and rank-preserving transformation, do not recover a useful routing signal on hard questions (best AUROC: 0.507). Cross-model comparison shows that larger parameter scale and higher base accuracy do not guarantee reliable confidence-based routing under specialist-domain difficulty shift. These findings challenge the premise of confidence-based adaptive RAG: in high-stakes biomedical settings, defaulting to always-retrieve is safer and more accurate than confidence-based routing when calibration on the target domain is unknown.

infographic.key_insight: Confidence-based retrieval fails on specialist biomedical questions, where confidence is nearly random but retrieval provides the largest accuracy gain.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For biomedical QA systems with unknown target-domain calibration, these results favor always retrieving evidence over confidence-based routing, without establishing clinical safety.
method: Compared adaptive and always-retrieve RAG across three biomedical QA benchmarks and multiple model sizes.
Tested five uncertainty signals, including token probabilities, sampling consistency, and verbalized confidence.
Evaluated five post-hoc calibration correction strategies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Confidence AUROC was 0.78–0.89 on standard exam questions but 0.506 on specialist questions, where retrieval improved accuracy by 11.2%; calibration corrections reached only 0.507 AUROC.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark accuracy does not establish real-world clinical safety; retrieval quality and target-domain performance still require validation.
infographic.paper_title: Confidence-Based Adaptive Retrieval Fails Where It Matters Most: A Paradox in Biomedical Question Answering

title: Comparative Study of Deep Learning Architectures for Brain Tumour Classification
authors: Prisha Gupta, Pradeep Kumar Gupta
abstract: Accurate and early classification of brain tumours from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for treatment planning, yet many published deep learning studies are trained and tested on small, single-source datasets, reporting accuracies that may not hold outside these datasets. This study compares six deep learning architectures for four-class classification (healthy, meningioma, glioma and pituitary tumour): a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN), an attention-based CNN, ShuffleNet, and EfficientNet-B0, ResNet-50 and Xception augmented with the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). The models were trained on a corpus assembled from four publicly available MRI datasets. Because these datasets carry no patient identifiers, a leakage-aware pipeline was developed that removes exact duplicates using MD5 hashing (550 images) and near-duplicates using perceptual hashing (8,024 images), and assigns visually similar images to the same fold during 5-fold group cross-validation. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) test on a fully held-out dataset was used to measure cross-dataset generalisation. Under a conventional random split, ShuffleNet achieved 97.1% accuracy with 1.2M parameters. Under leakage-aware group K-fold cross-validation, ShuffleNetV2 (98.41%) and EfficientNet-B0 (98.23%) were statistically indistinguishable (paired t-test, p = 0.19), and both significantly outperformed the custom CNNs. On the held-out dataset, accuracy dropped for every model: EfficientNet-B0 generalised best (78.4%), while ShuffleNetV2 fell to 66.2%. Glioma-meningioma confusion was the dominant error mode, and Grad-CAM maps showed that predictions were driven by tumour regions. These results indicate that in-distribution accuracy alone overstates real-world performance and that leakage-aware and cross-dataset evaluation should be reported alongside it.

infographic.key_insight: High within-dataset accuracy masked weaker cross-dataset performance: EfficientNet-B0 generalised best at 78.4%, while ShuffleNetV2 fell to 66.2%.
infographic.clinical_relevance: MRI tumour classifiers need robust external evaluation before their reported accuracy can inform expectations for clinical use.
method: Compared six deep learning architectures across healthy, meningioma, glioma and pituitary tumour MRI classes.
Combined four public datasets, removing exact and near-duplicates and grouping visually similar images for 5-fold cross-validation.
Tested cross-dataset generalisation using leave-one-dataset-out evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Leakage-aware cross-validation found ShuffleNetV2 (98.41%) and EfficientNet-B0 (98.23%) statistically indistinguishable (p = 0.19), but every model lost accuracy on the held-out dataset.
infographic.watch_item: Without patient identifiers, image-similarity grouping cannot guarantee patient-level separation between folds.
infographic.paper_title: Comparative Study of Deep Learning Architectures for Brain Tumour Classification

title: JECT: Addressing the Context Shortcut in Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for Chest CT
authors: Hanbin Ko, Hong-Jun Choi, Jihun Kim, Young-Gon Kim, Dongheon Lee, Chang Min Park
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting features of masked regions from visible context. In chest computed tomography, the findings that decide a diagnosis, such as a small nodule, are often not predictable from the surrounding anatomy. A hidden finding is then best predicted toward normal anatomy, and the prediction loss stops rewarding the encoder for representing it. We call this the context shortcut. Conditioning the predictor on the radiology report repairs the prediction, but in our setup the encoder gains little over image-only pretraining: the report supplies what the encoder never had to learn. JECT therefore gives the report two roles: a condition for the predictor and, through masked section-text prediction, a target for the encoder, which must predict the report's anatomical sections from the unmasked scan. A hierarchical three-dimensional encoder that predicts at every stage keeps this clinical content at every scale. In ablations, the text target improves classification and localization, while conditioning adds little to the encoder. Trained from scratch on 173k volumes, the recipe reaches the level of current computed tomography foundation models in classification, retrieval and nodule malignancy, and of task-specific models in lung-cancer risk prediction after fine-tuning. Conditioning still matters: its predictor can be reused, with no extra training, to show where a report sentence acts, changing most at the finding the sentence describes. Code and pretrained weights are available.

infographic.key_insight: JECT addresses the “context shortcut” in chest CT learning by making the encoder predict report content, encouraging it to represent findings that surrounding anatomy cannot predict.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support chest CT classification, finding localization, and risk prediction, but the abstract does not establish clinical readiness.
method: Condition masked-region feature prediction on the radiology report.
Train the encoder to predict anatomical report sections from the unmasked scan.
Apply prediction objectives at every stage of a hierarchical 3D encoder.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained from scratch on 173k CT volumes, JECT reportedly matched current CT foundation models across classification, retrieval, and nodule malignancy tasks, and task-specific lung-cancer risk models after fine-tuning.
infographic.watch_item: Report conditioning alone added little encoder benefit in this setup; implementation should preserve the text-target objective rather than assume report access is sufficient.
infographic.paper_title: JECT: Addressing the Context Shortcut in Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for Chest CT

title: A multimodal foundation model for tissue proteomics and morphology in cancer
authors: Benedikt von Querfurth, Lukas Klein, Cédric Vincent-Cuaz, Eeshaan Jain, Yexiang Cheng, Johann Wenckstern
abstract: Cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions increasingly rely on integrating tissue morphology with specific molecular readouts of the tumor and its microenvironment. H&E histopathology provides scalable morphology, whereas multiplex spatial proteomics quantifies dozens of proteins in situ with spatial context, but remains selectively deployed, often with different marker panels across cohorts. This creates a translational bottleneck: most patients lack high-depth molecular profiling, and existing models rarely integrate morphology and spatial molecular data in a single framework. We present VirTues-M2, a multimodal foundation model that jointly learns from H&E and spatial proteomics using a novel vision transformer-based architecture. By encoding marker identity during pretraining, VirTues-M2 is robust to missing modalities, imperfect modality pairing or registration, and variable marker panels, enabling unified inference for tissue phenotyping, panoptic cell segmentation, virtual staining, annotation-free biomarker discovery, and reinforcement learning-based adaptive marker panel selection to reduce assay burden. As a concrete demonstration of translational utility, in a newly collected cohort of 1,053 treatment-naive non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with paired spatial proteomics and H&E, VirTues-M2 discovers high-risk and low-risk tissue signatures that stratify overall survival in both the discovery cohort and an independent validation cohort, outperforming current state-of-the-art stratification schemes; all enabled by VirTues-M2's ability to jointly analyze both modalities within a single model.

infographic.key_insight: VirTues-M2 jointly learns tissue morphology and spatial protein patterns to support multiple cancer research tasks within one model.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The model identified tissue signatures associated with overall survival in NSCLC, suggesting potential for future risk stratification pending further clinical evaluation.
method: Combines H&E histopathology and multiplex spatial proteomics using a vision transformer architecture.
Encodes marker identity to accommodate variable protein panels, missing modalities, and imperfect image pairing or registration.
Supports tissue phenotyping, cell segmentation, virtual staining, biomarker discovery, and adaptive marker panel selection.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a newly collected cohort of 1,053 treatment-naive NSCLC patients with paired data and survival stratification in discovery and independent validation cohorts that outperformed current state-of-the-art schemes.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative performance estimates or prospective evidence that model-guided decisions improve patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: A multimodal foundation model for tissue proteomics and morphology in cancer
